newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City bomb victims recount horrors.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City bomb victims recount horrors.

text.p: A surgeon told of amputating a trapped woman's leg and a man said losing his wife drove him to the brink of suicide as witnesses described the horror of the Oklahoma City bombing to a jury considering whether convicted bomber Timothy McVeigh should be executed.

One by one, survivors and people who lost loved ones in the April 19, 1995, attack on the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, which killed 168 people, described their anguish for a jury of seven men and five women who were to decide if McVeigh should be put to death or spend his life in prison.
McVeigh, 29, was found guilty on Monday and prosecutors since Wednesday have presented often sad, graphic testimony aimed at persuading the jury to vote for the death penalty.

But federal Judge Richard Matsch also kept a rein on emotions. After Peggy Broxterman testified about her son Paul, she blurted out, "God bless America." Matsch later told the jury the remark, apparently aimed at influencing the jury, was inappropriate and should be disregarded.
The witnesses were both touching and heartbreaking as they revealed the depth of their losses.

Michael Lenz told the court his pregnant wife Carrie went to work early the day of the bombing so she could show co-workers ultrasound photos of her unborn child. He said her death left him devastated and contemplating suicide.
"There was a point where I actually stuck a pistol in my mouth. I couldn't pull the trigger, thank God," Lenz said.

Gregory Sohn, who lost his wife Vickey, said he continues to care for the children from her previous marriage as well as his own. "It was our family. I couldn't bear the thought of losing anybody else," Sohn said.
Kathy Youngblood said her husband John died after 23 days in a hospital. When he took a turn for the worse she was rushed out of the hospital room by physicians.
"That was the last time I saw John alive," she said.
The jury was shown a videotape demonstrating how P.J. Allen suffered chronic lung injuries and now breathes with difficulty.
Sharon Ice told the jury how patriotic her brother, Paul Ice, was. "He was so proud of being an American. Ever since he was a little boy he loved his country," she said tearfully.

Dr. James Sullivan said he crawled on his belly through the rubble to reach Daina Bradley, who was trapped in a crevice. At one point, the orthopedic surgeon said, he mistakenly thought the amputation was over only to find the leg was still connected.

"She was still attached and she screamed," he said, explaining that he was trying to perform the surgery quickly because of the instability of the collapsed building. He completed the operation with his pocketknife and the woman, who lost her mother and her two children in the bombing, survived.

Sharon Coyne said that she spent 12 hours on the day of the bombing looking for her infant daughter Jaci Rae, going from hospital to hospital, before finally returning home. The baby's body was found in the rubble of the building a week later. "I felt lucky I was able to hold her. I was very, very lucky," she said.

Oklahoma state epidemiologist Sue Mallonee told the jury injuries suffered by bombing victims included severe lacerations from glass cuts, a doorknob embedded in a woman's head, an ear torn away from the skull, the loss of an eye.

Susan Urbach told how her facial scar frightened a small child at church. But the scar now signifies recovery, she said. "You don't get your scar unless you've been wounded and you've healed," Urbach said. "It's my badge of honour."

Once prosecutors wrap up their part in the penalty phase, the defence will make an opening statement and call witnesses to try to persuade the jury to spare the Gulf War veteran's life and opt instead for life in prison without parole.
